title: Not the jug (Avot 4:20)
hook: look not at the flask, but at what is inside it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ben Zoma: gibor, the strong conquer their own urges, and the honored honor others. Your line was strong is self-mastered. Did you take the slow breath? Day two hundred sixty-seven.

At a wine shop, there's a bottle with a gorgeous label, heavy glass, a wax seal. And next to it, a plain bottle with a label that looks like it was printed at home. The hand drifts toward the fancy one. Sometimes what's inside is thin and sour, and the plain bottle would've been wonderful. People get sorted the same way. The young intern, the older colleague, the guy with the accent, the woman in the wrong clothes. Near the end of chapter four, two sages argue about exactly this, using jugs of wine.
screen: `THE FANCY LABEL.` → `THE PLAIN BOTTLE.` → `TWO SAGES, AND JUGS OF WINE.`

segments.voice: First, one sage says: learning from the young is like eating unripe grapes and drinking wine straight from the press. Learning from the old is like eating ripe grapes and drinking aged wine. Experience matters, he's saying. Go to the elders. Then Rabbi Meir answers him. Don't look at the jug. Look at what's in it. There's a new jug full of old wine, and an old jug that doesn't even have new wine in it. In other words: a young person can hold deep, mature wisdom, and an old person can be empty. The container tells you nothing for sure. You have to taste. The Bible says something close to this, when the prophet Samuel is choosing a king and is impressed by Jesse's tall eldest son, Eliab. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God tells him, "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." And the chosen one turns out to be the youngest, out with the sheep. Rabbi Meir lived this. His own teacher, Elisha ben Abuyah, later left the path of the sages, and the others called him simply acher, the other one. The Talmud asks how Rabbi Meir could keep learning from him, and answers with a picture: he found a pomegranate, ate what was inside, and threw away the peel. Not the jug. What's in it. That doesn't mean age and experience don't matter. It means you don't get to skip the tasting. Every person has to be met for what they actually hold.
screen: `UNRIPE GRAPES, OR AGED WINE?` · `A NEW JUG FULL OF OLD WINE.` · `GOD LOOKS ON THE HEART.` · `THE POMEGRANATE AND THE PEEL.` · then, large: `NOT THE JUG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look past one label. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've quietly sorted by their outside. Too young to know anything. Too old to get it. Too loud, too plain, too different. Picture their face. Now set the label down, and wonder what's actually inside them. What have they lived through? What might they know? Stay curious for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Rabbi Meir, whose rule was: don't look at the container, look at what's in it. A new jug can hold old wine, and an old jug may hold none at all.
Your line: you have to taste. Today, judge one thing, or one person, by what's inside instead of how it looks. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Rabbi Meir's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder not to judge people or ideas by appearance, age or background.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: don't look at the jug.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't judge a book by its cover.
what it means: age, looks and background don't tell you what someone holds. you have to taste.
what a scholar hears: Rabbi Meir is answering the sage just before him, who said learn from the old, and he lived it with his teacher Elisha ben Abuyah.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 1 Samuel 16:7 now JPS 1917, not KJV; 'tall, handsome son' corrected to Jesse's tall eldest son Eliab (the verse speaks of his countenance and height, not handsomeness); unsourced 'many refused to learn from him' replaced with what Chagigah 15b actually does (asks how Rabbi Meir could learn from Acher); 'every one of us does this' and 'most of us' removed from the hook.

Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: both sayings fall in 4:20 in the common numbering (4:26–27 in some editions); the first is by Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda of Kfar HaBavli, left unnamed here.
Some manuscripts attribute 'don't look at the jug' to Rabbi (Judah the Prince) rather than Rabbi Meir; the outline follows the common attribution to Rabbi Meir; confirm.
1 Samuel 16:7 is quoted from JPS 1917 (checked against the Mechon Mamre JPS text; identical wording). Eliab and his height: 1 Samuel 16:6-7; eldest: 1 Samuel 17:13.
Rabbi Meir and Elisha ben Abuyah, 'found a pomegranate, ate the inside, threw away the peel': Chagigah 15b; confirm.
David as the youngest, out with the sheep: 1 Samuel 16:11.
